PHYSIOLOGICAL LECTURE AT NV A RRINGTON.

On Tuesday evening, a second physiological lee- rum under the auspicesof the Co-operative Society, Wan given in Winivick-st. Co-operative Ilan, by the Freisstotb of Macclesfield, the subject of the Ictare being “The circulation and respiration " Dr. Adams presided, and there wan a fair atten- dance.

The Clt A IRM AN, who was received With applause. said it afforded him the greatest pleasure to take the chair that night at a lecture which to closely concerned himself and his own profession ; and lie was only too glad to do en when a lecture of popular character was to be given in language which--- he said it in all humility --was hound to be better understood than the same lecture would be if given by a medical man himself, for their lecturer knew precisely what he wanted to teach them, and the precise form in which any would desire it to he put, whereas medical men and scienti- fic men were far too apt to take it for granted that the audience were fully acquainted with the mean- ing of the majority of the terms they had to use. ( Hear, hear.) The subject of the lecture was one of vital interest. They could not get along very well without circulating arid respiring,and yet they were always liable to accidental injuries, which interfered with these vital functions A knowledge of the natural course and distribution of the blood vessels was, therefore, very important if they wished to be able to give any assistanav to those who might receive severe injuries. With regard to respiration, the cause of drowning was the suspen- sion of respiration, no that the air could not get to the lunge. The problem, then, for them to deal with in a case like that was the restoration of the function of breathing. These, however, were , matters which would, perhaps, be treated by Mr. I Freeston, upon whom he called to give his lecture. Mr. Fuessrox, who woo cordially received, then gave I an interesting lecture which was closely followed by his audience. He mentioned that the heart, the organ of I eirculation, was a muscle or a number of muscles corn- pacted together, and by therontractionof t..ese muscular fibres motion was given to the blood, which was thus I circulated through the body. The purpose of the cir- nolation FRS to carry new vitalising and nutritive I material to all parts of the body. The bloid was .metimes called the o vital fluid " because it got a fresh supply of nutriment from the food and a fresh supply of oxygen from the air. The blood , having been put into good condition it carried nourish- ment to all the organs of the boly,leaving a bit here and ' there, wherever the organs were a hit worn oat; it also picked up waste material, little particles of matter, of moisture or gas or other material that had been worn off and done with, and which if allowed to stop in the sys- tem would accumulate and engender disease. Having alluded to the constituents of the blood, he said the tem- perature of the body wasalways high«, than the tempera- ture of the enter atmosphere. They put their clothes on to prevent radiatien of the heat from the body, but lithe halt was always warmer than the atmosphere and if the i heat was always radiating how was that heat kept up? Niue-tenths of the heat of the only was produced by chemical action. There was a progress going on in the lungs not in the bully very similar to the process that goes only their fire-places when they had a fire on. Coal contained a large amount of carbon and hydrogen and in the fresh air, which they must have for a fire to burn, there was oxygen. lathe process of combustion the oxygen of the air united with thecarbon and hydrogen of the coal with stick force that heat and light were evolved, no that heat woo produced by chemical action. The same thing trad, place in our bodies only owing to moisture in the body they did not get light. The lec- turer then referred to ambulance work which he highly approvssl of. He alot gave some valuable hints as to Site treatment of the drowned. Alluding to iionsuinp- lion, he said it was a terrible thing when consumption got into a family, but they should not too soon conclude that it notnsoite inevitable that they would go oil in eonsumption. The hest thing they could do, if they bad reason to think they might be tainted with consumproo, watts set about in an intelligent manner bigot a know- ledge iii the laws of health, and though they might sot ultimately cure the disease lie knew for a fact that they might ward it off for years and years. He himself had been told nearly 40 yearsago that he was in consomption—(latighter)—aud One inedi- cal gentleman told him that, with care, he might live Its years longer. (Laughter and applause,) The CHAIHNIAS said the lecture which Mr. Freestrin had delivered hail been of a very charming and instruc- tive character,and intricate and technical facts had been placed before the audience in language which their repented plaudits proved had been thoroughly under- stood and grasped. As lie remarked in his opening speech, he was only too glad to know that there were men outside his own pretension who took up these sub- jects and dealt with them in a popular and nontechnical spirit. it sometimes happened that there wore leaders among them who had the power of simple lan- guage, who were them.ilves men of exceptional scientific knowledge and skill, but they were the exceptions, and by no means fanned the rule. As a rule it was a greater pleasure bi listen to a lecture on a technical subject dealt with in the popular manner which had been adopted by Mr. Freeston that evening. (Applause.) The Chairman gave some valuable hints on first aid to the injund, and remarked that if they could not atop the bleeding by ambulance rules, they could stop it by rule of thumb, and the best rule of thumb was their own thumb. (Laugliter and applause.) In other words they could stop it by sticking their thumb into the wound and keeping it there. There was no bleeding from any part of the body which could not I»t arrivrted by proie-rly and deeply applied pressure, where.' ever it was. (Applause.) lie also supplemented by some further advice Mr. Freeston's remarks with regard to tl,e t_tratment rI the apparently. drowned. ' "

Mr. eItITCHLXV moyed-ii rote ))f thanks to the lectur- er for his instructive address, and expressed the hope that the muss of lectures would be carried through. (Applause). He was only sorry that the wwking-classes of the town did not take more interest in those science lectures. He thought they ought to do so fee their own benefit. (Hear. hear). Mr. T. Illeessix seconded the Vote of Ulnas to the lecturer and chairman, which was carried with acclam- ation.

The announcement of the death on Monday morning of Mr. T. A. Walker, the contractor for the Manchester Ship Canal, has been received with gen- eral regret. The anti opinion of Sir John hawk' thaw stood Mr. Walker in great nicest in the future, and it was owing to the confidence which the distinguished engineer reposed in the contractor that Mr.;: Walker was afterwards entrusted with the more extensive and ardu- ous work of the constroction of the Severn Tunnel. When, in 1879, the d inut ors of the Great Western Railw sy Company, alarmed at an irruption of water into the drif two, or small gallery, under the Severn, near Port- skewett, on which they had been then engaged for nearly seven years, asked Sir John Ilawkshaw to take charge of the wort.n as chief engineer, that gentleman agreed to do so only on the condition that he should be allowed to let the works to someone it whom he could have confi- dence, and on their eonsent he rant for Mr. Walker. Amongst these may be mentioned the Prince of Wales Dock at Swans., the Potent. Some excitement was occasioned in St. Helens on Saturday night, by a rumour that there had been a painfully sudden death at one of the local football matches. Unhappily there was some foundation for the report. It seems that, immediately after the conclusion of the St. Helens Recreation v. Stookport match in liounilary-rilad, one of the spectators , a young man, named William Myers, who had just ememed from the field, and wa.s on his way home along !Campbell-At., was Seen to stagger and fall to the ground. i Several people ran to his assistance, and blood was found to be issuing from his nose and mouth. lie was removed ito his home n Tontine-st., and Dr. Mouton wax sum- moned. On that gentleman's immediate arrival he pro- nounced Myers to be dead. The deceased who was 28 years of age had formerly been employed as a mixer at one of the glass works but had been off work for nearly 12 months inconsequence of ill-herilth. He bad during , that period been under the care of Dr. Williams, of Liver- pool. On Saturday, in Court of Appeal, judgment was given in this appeal of the defendant Company from the • decision of Lord Justice Bowen, at the trial at Middlesex holding that the defendant company was still hound to pay to the plaintiff the biennial rent of £lO.OOO in res- pect of two coal inines—the Yard and the Arley Mines —situate near Wigan, until such time as all the coal in the Arley Mine was gotten and paid for. The Master of the ROlll4, at the eons:lesion of the arguments, said the plaintiff had in this ease brought an action against the defendants in which he contended that, under an agree- ' ment in the nature of a Bow, the defendant company ' undertook to work thornless, soasto produce in two years £lO,OOO. The plaintiff said in effect that as the defend- ants had worked the mines short of that amount they were bound to make up the difference between the coals actually gotten and the £lO,OOO payable every twoyears. The defendant company admitted that this was the meaning of the lease; bat they said that, in considera- tion of the money they bad paid atnntly--some £87,000 —they no re not hound to any any rent beyond £3,000, • as the amount of money they had already paid more j than covered the value net upon the Arley Mine, the most valuable of the two. The defendants relied upon a previews in page 16 of the lease in support of this view ; but in order to give it the interpretation measure to support their cans, they read that proviso in connection with another to be found upon page 21 of the agreement. What the court had to do was to construe the proviso— the first .111 he had alluded to—according to the ordin- ary grainmatieal construction of the English language as applied to ouch a subject as coal mines. That prow sion or proviso, which applied to the present ease, read leneeo shall, in every two years' until the whole of the Arley Mine hereby deiiiked shall have been paid for" (the counsel for the appel'ant stopped there, but proviso read on;—" at the footage rent aforesaid." The footage rent of £75 an acre was dreeribed elsewhere. The to-utak, rent was the rent Le coal which had been gotten. The defendants had nestended that it did not matter how the Arley inine was paid for, no long as the full amhint of the value WM paid by them; but this siew could not be upheld ; the reduced rent of £3,000 could not come into force until the value of it had been met or paid for by the coals actually gotten in that mine. The counsels for the defendants were not justified in reading another peonies into the one cited, bee. ause it related to another method of paying for the inints—by any watts whatever. Mr. Collins, in arguing the case for the appellants, had coin- ;stained of the hardship that had beets Unposed upon the defendants by the view taken by Lord justice Bowen ; that was not exactly the question—the only question being the proper and true construction of Use lease. Ile (Lord Esher', however, must say that he considered the person who drew up the instrument between the parties had gone to the very edge of powers of the lessor fertile, and no doubt the intention wants getao muchaa possible out of the lewes in the interest of the lessor for life. No provioa on the least relating to the payment for Arley Mine stood atone; and it wa.s the folly part of the dred which dealt with the obligation to pay this £lO,OOO of a rental, and with the reduction of it to £3,000. The interpretation of the Lord Justice in the court below n-no right, and the appeal inust be dismissed with costs.— Lord Justice Lindley concurred. Be said he raw no hard- ship in the matter if the defendant company loyally .repted the basins of the lease and slid what they could to get the coals cif the Arley Mine. In that case the nut in respect to the Yard Mine would he o.nly£3,ooo.—Lord Justice Lopes agreed with this decnion.—Mr. Henn boflino .Ised fie a stay of execution, pending an appeal to the House of Lords—The Master of the Rolls: mush ini;ney is at stake ?—Mr. C,mltins Between £5,000 and £6,ooo.—The Master of the Rolls: Roth parties are solvent, and therefore we see no reason why execution , should be stayed.

Early on Mollll2ly morning, the body of a man, then unknown, was found hangmg by the neck in AAlitolis-yard, 01.1-road. Latchford, front n clot hes iine that was fastened to the muffler that he was wearing. The discovery WU made by I'. iistable Millington, who was patrolling the neighbourhood. It was at tint rumoured that the man was a victim of murder, but the police. alter examining the rant, came to the conclusion that it with a caseof A wound over the left eye is supposed to have Ix en caused by the head ot the deceased coming into contact with the wall, on which there were blood stains.

On Wednesday. Mr. 11. C. Yates, coroner, attended at the Norton Anus Inn, Wilderspool-road, to inquire into the circumstatims id the death. Constable Millington said that at about 2.35 on the ! morning of Monday he was working hi+ but whirli extended to the Old-road, Latchford. Ile went into Ashton's yard, and on turning on his right he discovered ! the hgly of a man hanging by a rope. His feet were touching the ground. If was suspended by a roue that had bum put through the muffler that he was wearing. ' The muffler had been twined twice round the neck, and the rope wm fastened to tar staple in the wall. At a little distance trot° the body—at a rough guess :thud thirteen yards away—svitnem now a pool of blood. Lying close bywas a coat. There were drops of blual in different parts of the yard. Witness satisfied himself that deceased was perfectly ilead—The Coroner : had you , also notice thecurious faint that the tongue was not pro- I truding front the mouth ?-IVitness Yrs ; the body was I partially warm. In answer to further questions front the I Coroner, witness mid that the clothes of the deceased were not disarranged, and that there were no signs of a ; struggle having taken place. Witnms cut down the body, and called in Dr. Smith. Witness had relieved his brother officerat 2.30, and he reported that everything : was right. The derexsed was It stranger to , Then' was no one ahatt at the time that witness found I the bidy. Over the left eye of the deceased there KM a ! out, and blood was wiring from at—Pa Juror It was a very wet night, which would make the blood appear more than was really the ram. Dr. Starkey Smith.depostsl that he was called to seethe body of the deceased shortly before four o'clock on Mon- day morning, by Inspector Spinks. Ile got to the place about four o'clock, and made an exuniartion on the body. There was a wound over the left eye, about three-quarters of an inch long. Witnem pasmd his finger into the wound, anal found that it hail gone down to the bine *Die bine was not injured. There were no marks of viirlenciton the: testy. The necktie was fasteoed twice niund tbe neck of the elmeased, and the onder coil was very tight. The tongue was not protruding, which was it pecnliar sympton. In the cases of stran- gulation the tongue was generally protruding, and remained no. Witness hail made a pist-mortem. The body was that of a man of about 45 or 48 years of age, very spare. There were no marks of violence, except those previously mentioned. The right side of the heart was choked up with blood. The stomach contained nearly one pint of water fluid, more like ginger-beer or lemonade titan anything else. All the other orgaru were empty. There was no injury to the head. Witness wm of opinion that the came of death was strangulation by luteging.—The Coroner Do you think the injury wag selfdaflicted ? —Witness 7 I think so; there ware no marks indicating that any struggle hail taken place at all. I examined carefully for that.—The Coroner Your theory is that the man first of all fastened the rope, and then arrareglislltim- self.—Witness You, sir; the lardy was of sufficient weight to do that. The necktie was tied just above the wind-pipe.—The Coroner : Did he seem to have been a dissipated man ?—Witness His organs did not point to that. lie looked as though he had been short of food, and them was marcely any fat on the body. There was no food in the stomach. Deceased looked like a seafaritixe man.—A Juror How long would it tare to strangle him B—Witness : I should think seven or eight minutes. There was no dislocation of the vertebne. Deceased died from pure strangulatiar. If there had been a sudden drop the neck would have been dislocated John Jones, Latchford, mid that he had known deceased by sight for something like twenty years, and had during that perhsi seen hint working at farmhouses. lie lard always gone by the name of Brackett, sod wit- ness never heard him Marled by any other name. Deceased was an Irishman, but witness did not know where he mune from, or what his age was. Deceased always spent what he got; in drink, witnms thought. Witness knew deceased generally heed on drink. Ile was stubborn in his way when he had drink, but was quiet when sober. Inspector Spinks, of the borough police force, spoke to having been called to see the body by Millington. The face of the deceassl was covered with blood. Witness examined the body minutely. Close to where the IxsW lay there was no blood, but witness saw a pool of blood in another part of the yard and fund the cap produced on a grid chose to. Blood was running down the incline into the grid. The cloth. of the &Teased was mturated with wet. The staple to whirli the rope was attachul was close to the back door of a dwelling-house, and there wa.s alight in a window. Th,•• body, which was removed to the Norton Arms, was dressed in a brown coat, two old vests, and two pairs of trousers. In the pockets were a quantity of tea and sugar, a piece of tobacco a I purse containing Is. Ed, and a tobacco box. On the : wall witness found marks of blood, and two or three hairs corresponding with those on the brow. In answer to the jury witness ,said that he thought that the cut on the fon'head was caused by deceased having come into I contact with the wall.

div.head: MURDER AND SUICIDE IN NORTH LONDON.
div.p: MURDER AND SUICIDE IN NORTH LONDON.

-• —• • A shocking tragedy occurred on Thursday night A Dalston London, Mrs. South, of Shrubland-grave, reperted to have murdered her two daughters, aged twelve and 14 years, by beating out their brains with a ; hammer. She then cut her own throat with a knife, and I died soon afterwards at the German Hospital, 'Mkt.- lane. She is supposed to have been inune.—The house i in which the tragedy WV enacted is in a •pliet part of I Shrubland-road, and was occupied by George South, and his family, consisting of his wife, Annie South, aged forty-eight, and their two datigkters, Ada, aged fourteen,. and Edith, ag,l twelve. 'Mere wa.s also a lodger named I Holloway and his wife in the limo.. The dreadful tragedy was diseoven4 by Mr. South ; himself on his return home from business at seven o'clock in the evening. On opening the door of the kitchen he was startled and horrified to see his wife ; sitting in a chair bleeding from an open wound in her ; I throat, and his two children lying at her feet with their ; heads 'battered and covered with blood. Inspector ; Cockerel" on searching the house, found that the children ; had been most brutally murdered with a hesvy claw I 'sunnier. A blood-stained razor was f•mnd near the I , inother, and no doubt was the weapon with which she I destroyed herself. The motive for the crime is unknown I The parents had lived happily together, aTla belt child- ren were bright, intelligent girls. Mrs. South had latterly I ; complain,' of pains in her head.

1 An INSURANCE CAIVE.—Ntrs. Hardy, 31. Nieholson-st., sued the Pearl Life 30, dance Company for £8 18s., be- ing an amount alleged to he due under a policy of Assu- rance effected upon the life of her husband.—Mr. Davies appeared for the plaintiff, and the del...den: company was represented by Mr. W. Swift, of St. Helens. Mr. Davies, in opening the case, said that in October, 1887, his client effected an insurance on the lives of her huoband and ton. Mr. Holt, the collector, gave her two policies. The proposal form was not signed 1 by her, but was made out by the collector. The questions , and answers, that had to be in writing, wore I written by the collector, who also signed Cie name of the proposer, although the was able to write. At the time of the proposal the plaintiff's 1 husband was under the rare of the doctor, but the collector maid that did not matter—he would live for I many a year yet. Weekly payments were continued up Ito the time of his death, which I,ecurred in August of , this year. On application being made to the company I for payment it woo refired.—Mr. Swift submitted that if ; snch was the case, there was no contract between the 1 company and the proposer as the propotat wan the contract—Mr. Davies contended that there , was a contract, as the -.policies were handed over. and the preminnit had been paid by the plain. tiff from Oct.. 1887, up to the time of her husbamiti death in 1889.—His Honour ruled that as there was a proviso in Hie policy stating that if the imured was suffering at the Dine of the proposAl from my bodily ailment, and it was not disclosed by the pro poser, then the proposer could not claim anything under the policy. He agreed that there had been a part per- formance of the contract by the handing over of Ole pdicy, and the payment of the premiums, and asked whether Mr. Swift wan prepared, or behalf of the com- pany, to repay the premium's—Mr. Swift said that tie company had offered to do no, but, the offer having been " refused, they now declined to renew it.--His Honour !etiolated that in that ease he should reserve his de.a- mon _

Considering that the Sultan is over head and ears in debt, and cannot oven pay his troops, it was a piece of what the Yankees would call " darned impudence" to spend £:150,000 in entertainments and presents to the Emperor and Eimlress of Germany. It would he a good thing for Turkey, and some other countries, if sundry Sovereigns could be shipped off after the manner of the Ex- Emperor of Brazil.

Tins news of the death of Mr. I The late Mr.T. A. Walker. THOMAS ANDREW WALKER, con- tractor of the Manchester Ship I !Canal, has been everywhere received with all ex- l pression of more than ordinary regret. We had known for some weeks that lie was solf,rinz from a dangerous complication of disorders; but it WM deemed desirable alike in his own interest and in the interest of the great work he had m hand,not to give publicity to the report which reached us. With the foresight which characterised him in all his un- dertakings, he had made provision for !such a con- tingency as has arisen ; and it is a matter of course therefore to Ray that his death will not pot a stop, even for a time, to the making of the Canal. II was a comparative stranger to this part of the 1 country before the Ship Canal project took form ; I lbut, as soon as the work commenced, it was 11 I seen that he cared for the thousands of mei. lin his employ as something more than mere machines for the execution of a colossal task. Ho was not called upon to take thought for the comfort, the education, and the spiritual neede ;of the navvies ; lost he did take thought, and lit is no small mead of praise fogey that he was in consequence known as "The Navvy's Friend." ; When engaged in constructing the Severn Tunnel —one of the greatest engineering feats of modern times--a church capable of accommodating 1,500 ' persons was burnt down. Within a month, we are told, he had another structure erected which would hold 2.0(K/ When the Barry Backs were !opened, he preferred to go to a dinner to 2,000 navvies rather than attend the banquet provided ,by the Railway Company. It was this prannal regard for men whiek endear.al lain to them-- a feeling which was heightened by his solicitude for those who were injured, and for the families of those nom killed in his employ. In the engineer- ing world, he was known as a great contractor, with an experience which was almost unrivalled ' for he had been engaged in North America, and South America, in Egypt and in Russia, an well as in his own country. Lancashire and Cheahire would have delighted to do him honour had he lived to 800 his mighty work completed. But it • was not to he. He has died with haniesa on his , Mick. The nation loses a great Captain of In- dustry ; and it loses more than that -it loses a man who was 00 peal as he was great.

The second part of the letter of Mr. Stems Lewis has reference to the way in which con- stables are made use of as watchers for poachers. Previous to his election, he stated that" a police- man had informed him that he was for 28 con- secutive nights watching for poachers, whilst his regular beat was neglected." As the information was given in confidence, Mr. Lewis declined to comply with the Chief Constables request for the name <4 his informant. But, he aids, as Colonel Hamm eastev was then anxious to investigate such a condition of affairs I will now ask him—

II) If he is aware that on or about the end of Sept-saber last, the whole of the police were drafted out of Runcorn—a town of nearly 20900 inhabitants - together wills all the police from the surrounding country districts--to watch for poachers at Norton. and that they did so watch from eleven at night till six the next morning. leaving the town and district of Runcorn absolutely unprotected? (2) If tie circumstance was not duly reported to him he next day by Superintendent Large? . ..-..--.. In connection with the Liverpool and North :1 Wales District of Methodist Free Churches, a temperance convention was held in Ellesmere-st. . Chapel, Runcorn, on Monday. The Rev. George Thompson presided, and representatives were pre- sent from Northwich. Norley. Widnes, Runcorn, Frodshana, Ilelsby, Barrow, Kingsley, &c. The . Every good ), Catrie wan God's Cause, and every entree that was not good was of the devil, and if they might judge of the drink traffic by its fruits it WAS of the desilj because the outcome of it wasesil and injury to the • highest interests of society. GREAT FIRE IN AMERICA.-120 FACTORIES DESTROYED.

A great fire broke out at noon, on Tuesday, at Lynn. Massachusetts. The contlagratein raged furiously for nearly eight hours, it being half-part SeYell in the evening before it finally burned itself out. 'rho scents of the famous Chicago and Raton Nes were re-enacted. Mothers were fleeing deinicatrieken with their babies in their arms, and indescribable confusion prevailed. Elle military patrolling tbe streets, and making vain efforts to restore order. A square toile of buildings were destroyed, including four banks and several churelies, lour newspaper offices, and a number of club houses. The Central Station id the Boston and Maine Railway was aim, horned to the gr.loll' I The losses in busbies; vytions, where twelve bityks sit the largest snoe factor- ies, as well as numerals stores, have been laid in ruins, is estimate-I at £2,000,030. principal dwelling- lionsw, burned were IlleSelocaupied by the isiorer classes,. and who see now being sheltered in the remaining churches and school hisisiv. Some buildings were blewn up with dynamite ill order to keep the her from spread- ing, N. hill. the city tire brigade was assisted in its efforts by engines from Roston, rialem, Ont.., and other places the vicinity. In all 120 factories, some of large sine, and 142 dwell- ing-honses have been consumed. These buildings con- : stituted 154 blocks, of whirl) 42 were of brick and stone, , and 112 of wood. The Mayor of Lynn has toned an appeal for funds to relieve -the distntss. That this will be gnat and widespread may lie gathered front the fact , that 8,000 people Will Ile forced ti forego their usual work and toms warily lose their means of livelihood.

div.p: ALLEGED MANSLAUGHTER BY A PRISoN WARDER.

Anthony Mitchell, a supernumerary warder at the ri Strangeways Prison, has lawn apprehended on a charge , of oiusing the death of William Henry Oatliffe, who was I in tie prison for drunkennomi and disorderly conduct. j From the evidence given at the conmer's inquest, on I Toeslay, it appears that at the time of his arrival in I ' prism Gatliffe was in fair, good lomith, 'nit as he was I ' sutTeriug from incipient delirium tremens, he was put by I the surgeon's direction in the prison Itapital, where, 1 according to custom, he was bound down with shoes. I so that he might not injure hitnself. On Friday night I IMitchell was left in charge of the hospital, in *he'll, in 1 j addition to tiatliffe, them were confined William bakes,. j who is charged with the murder of George Orion, at 1 Bury ; Chadwirk, who is under suspition of having ' murdered a pawnbntker's assistant at Atherton: and a ; man named Maclure, who was on Tuesday, at the Assinm, convicted of manslaughter. Those prisonsrs gave evidence, on Tuesday, to the effect that during Friday night and the small hours on Satuniay morning, Gatliffe was in a deli..ra state and making a great noise, and because he refused to be quiet the warder , gagged bim, struck him repeatedly and violently with I 1 his fists, and otherwise maltreated him. While the blows were bring administer," Mitchell. it is said, made , use of some thnsttening expressions. One of thew, woo the encoun- ter between Warrington and Broughton at Broughton, which was ahandonwl in the early part of the second half. Tile "A " teams of these two organiamions playea their game out at Warrington, the hoinesters winning very easily by three goals four tries and seven minors to two minors.

The game with Burton-on-Trent is looked forward to as one of the plosmantest on the Runcorn and and the match that took place, on Raturvlay, realised expert, bons. Brilliant open play was theonler of thio day, and both teams shone in their own particular department. Sir, rhe Scleiflnlacher was again tile topic of canner- sati in at the last Boaal meeting, of the Runcorn Colon— who sent in his sisigiotion according to Mr. Aaron's proposal made some two Board days ago. Mr. D. If. Jonew, condemning the policy of Mr. Aaron's prismedings, made a 'mist pertinent remark when he observed that it was preposterous to allow Mr. Aaron to proceed with his motion, in the face of the fact that the Board then sitting was the steeliest number he had ever sat ou— tfight members only—and out of that number he isiinted out that there were four known members who were the Workhouse Master's friends—that Mr. Stokes, another member, had left before the voting came on. Himself (Mr. &ems) and Mr. Baguley,another member, atsteined front voting On account of the unfair proca,dings going on, leaving the fate of the schoolmaster in the hands of est guardian only (Mr. Lewis) Si, decide. There arc 140111 e 45 members on that Board who should have bl,lll duly notified of the proceedings, if Mr. Aaron had oboyisi the rule laid down by the Chairman, that all important matters must be duly given notice of. The whisihmister having complied with Mr. Aaron's proposal—tendered his resignation, the Boned my he is at liberty to again apply for the situation if lie chooses to don. The Lawriusdi inquiry re the alleged neglect of Relieving, Officer ex. narrated the officer from all blamed—Yours, be. A RATEAYER.

A CIIIRP FROM A RUNCORN SPARROW. Sir,—At a meeting of the Board of Guardians, held at Dutton on the sth inst., amongst other matters for dis- cussion was the censure by the Coroner's Jury, at Run- corn, of the Relieving Office (Mr. Ward) for neglect in not providing necessary medical advice for a young man named Lawrenson, who died from typhoid fever at Bryotrest., Runcorn, after an illnesseatending over three weeks. The evidence given at the inquest was to the effect that the relieving officer, after being informed that the man was in urgent need of medical attention, died of neglect. It was known that Or. Mangan,who had Ives attending this young man, had actually refused any furffier attendun.,. I may aISO state that the doctor was also censured for votsing in his attendance and advice before seeing that the deceased was under the care of the wit Doctor. Erns nnfortunate young man was coOrely witlikot Medical atWdion or advice for thrne previous to Jtis &all. Nem& taoaose tie was devoid of the necessary funds to pay a doctor. The caroller, as well as the jury, uonsiderol it 6 very sad case and thought themselves perfectly justitual afass- ing the centtoreS they did. At, this meeting of the cittay, tans mentioned ahoy*, one of the worthirn, Mr. Aaron, the member for Weston, designates OW lazy tut 80 many klarrows—here to-day and gone to-morrow. Now to inform Mr. Aaron that the greater yarnon of the or are natives of Runcorn and ratepayers, and that the remainder of them have been ratepayers in Runcorn for many years, and such remarks from him cannot there- , fore he taken as anything but an insult to the jury, who conscientiously did their duty and no more. Su now, Mr Aar), the jury are men of respect abitity, well- known in Runc,trn, and their capabilities and intelligence are certainly eynal tothase who term jorymen as spar- rows, be they members of the Board of Guardians or not.—Yours truly,
AAL,orpS SPARROW O. 2.

BIBLE, BistioP. BEER, NOVELS. Sir,—From the papers. I sae Bishop Jayne, in a recent speech at Stockport, said—" He would like to own and manage a public-house, he would like bi be able to write a first-rate novel.- I fail to see that tuck a desire is compatible with the office of a Biitlintl his chief duty accordingto his ordination is to be a faithful shepherd of souls, preach the word of God, instant in and out of season, to encourage his flock to flee every appearance of evil. Verily, drink and its attendant evils are some of the greatest curses of this land. Where one man has an iron will to govern his appetite, there are thousands who fall through the temptation coming in their way. Far better a Bishop to set the example of total abstinence than publicly make such remarks. Drunkenness is a sin a the flesh and it is fearful to read, No drunkard shall inherit the kingdom of God." The democracy may well eXClairll, "Church and Beer go hand in hand." What am the general results of novels ? As a nil,' they are not of an elevating character ; tend to fill our prisons ; empty our places of worship fill the mind with pleasures which are only for a season ; wean the rising generation from laying hold of the good tidings, en brac- ing Christ by a living faith. The Bishop would serve his day and generation to greater benefit by studying Paul's advice "To know nothing among you, save Jesus Christ and him crucified, not ashamed of the gospel of Christ, for it is the power of God unto salvation." Not a word here about tradition or novels. The masses may well keep away from Church when they read what the heads of it are teaching, with their silly innovations, early celebrations, floral decorations, auricular confelions, baptismal regeneration, Virgin Mary.images, crucifixes, crosses. he.. set up for adoration. The word of God must reign above all things, rnd remain the judge of all men." I Luther.)—Yours respectively, ROBERT FOULKES. Frodsham, Nov. 25th, 1889.

div.head: OUR NATIONAL _POVERTY. AND. TIIE LAND
div.p: OUR NATIONAL _POVERTY. AND. TIIE LAND
FOR TIIE PEOPLE.

- - SOL—This question is coming to the front—full time I that it did. I have been for many years hammering at it in one way or other and formy pains I have been des- cribed as a would be " spoliator," " a robber," a divider of other minis goods," Ise, ne. ; to a great extent isolated as holding and preaching an impractieable doctrine. I am not alone now. I scarcely pick up a paper hut I C.OMP across an article of more or less length denouncing the present system or suggesting a way by which the land of this country may be held, managed, met cultiva- ted for the benefit of the many—for the poriple—instead of for the few, The Liberal press denounces and even the Tory press apoli igLies and promises on behalf of the party "1 great nwasore of land reform." Who believes it? My knowledge of that party during SO years of political life is such that I know they give the people no' king until it is extorted from them. he measure of land reform thaf the For party will give no we need not look for—but when a measure of reform iowrenehesl from them, they turn round and bow of their gener- osity, and .y we gave you repeal of the corn laws— extension of the borough franchise—and later still, enfranehised two millions of county voters. It requires no elm!l amount of barefaced impudenre to make thine false assertions, and by-and-by, after a political struggle such as we seldom we, they will again boast of their generosity and say we gave you the rotornt of the land flstS laws. there will be a hard fight for it, no there is for every measure of reform, and why! The land is in too few hands—a powerful and gigantic would have ug, believe that what tied has given for the nation nt large should be held and controlled by the few for their own sole benefit and pleasure 'Mere are 28 , dukes slim own 3,981,811 acres ; 33 mardnia!M 55W0, or bold, 1.582,288 asset; 174 earls with 5,882,218 acres; 52

viscounts with over 796,000 aims.; 218 barons with 3,850,180 acres. Thus we have 505 men owning mid controlling 15,000,000 acnw of land eight millions cd which, as common land, they have stolen fmm the people during the last 120 years.; and with what result ? Agricultund villages have been depopulated ; and the land is gone out of cultivation. Our able-bodied MOO have emigrated to distant shores, Those who could not emigrate have gone into the towns to reduce wages and increase poverty then.. It Ism been acute with the agricultural labourer of "anywhere, anywhere out of the world "--out of the agricultural world at least • any- where where he can get any sort of wire's, and is inane of ROMA kind. Landlords talk of their rights ;it is time that the is everty-stri,•ken toilers spoke of their wrong.‘, and dein:mil...l their rights--the right to live by their labour—not the right to adopt Lord Salishur's cure fir their poverty, to emigrate. Let Lord :Salisbury and the 500 mot who 4abtrol 15 million aloes of land emigrate as osm as imasitile, and the country will help thole. No iI'SR a man than Lord Derby has wild that if the land of this country was praperly coltivated, it wool.' produce £80,000,000 worth of hasl annitallv, more tluoi lit does at present. To do that would minim a vast 1 amount •if labour of a variol kind ; the farm labam.r, the wheelwright, the .• h, the agricult oral implement i maker. In fact every trade would share in the expentli- ' tore:aid distribution lir this vast sum, and the milli.. 1..1 men the the pn•sent vicious spats]] has witlitit'awn ; from agrieulture, avonld be restored to their old lamas and Old o,lllsntio/1. rhe comps:psi districts would be relievol, eVery mill and every fm•tory wauld be set going, ; dying industries wintld be. n•vivetl, and new would spring, into existent•e, and general pnwperity would ensue. We should he independent of the ionizing ' for our food supply to avers' great extent, if not alto- gether-4. 5 eonsimuna hat devoutly Si be wished." don't think anybody would be the morsel 1,11 the landowner. 1 have never know anyone the worse justice being Ilona` all round. There will always be a ' demand for land under equitable circumstance, and the demand will he likely to outrun the supply. , What is wanting is security and fixity of tenure, at flue rent, avith comperwation for improvements t•lTectol by the tenant. I haven° faith in the natant:Mx:Dion of tflo Land. I see no necessity for it, and should not like SO have the State for a hn.hont ; but would prefer as far as ownership goes the preo•nt with the•ir Igtwers Cir mischief taken away. Let Sinew hop what Siren have on fair terms, gone laws abolishol, and the land they cannot manage managed he others, they getting their fair share of the produce. am sir, yours respectfully, Sankey Bridges, Nsv. 26th, 1883.

div.head: TEETOTALISM AND LONOEVITY.
div.p: TEETOTALISM AND LONOEVITY.

Sir,--sonnt statistics of the British MediutlAssestiation, earsfrilly edited by Dr. Isambard Owen, and first breirsht ! before the public at the Dublin meeting of that body mow than two years ago, have recently been n'-produeed in the" Revue Seientilique " a French paper, and quoted by some of the press of this country for purposes for ; which they were never intended, and have invariably • been confuted. They have also been referred to at "trade" rueetings to frighten the teetotallers, and to encourage the drinkers. By these figures an attempt Ira.. been made to prove that the " intemperate,'" free ; drinkers," " careless drinkers," and ta mperate, live I longer than the ahstainers. It,. Owen, as the editor, ; affirms that he does not take this view of the statistics, land rwaftirms as recently at, October 30th in letters tn the" Globe," and the" Daily Telegraph," in which he • writes," In drawing up this report, I pointed out at some ; length that the figunts representing the average age at ; death of the total abstainers, did net admit of direct wanparison with tly other figures in the table,and:statesl in , rlain terinsthat no conclusion auto the relative longevity ; ;oh abstainers, and temperate drinkers cuuld warrantably be drawn from it." Awl the " Lancet " of April 13th I says—. By dint of quoting Ow figures and omitting the wpially important context, some spokesmen of litpur selling interest, have, claimed to assure the public on medical authority that total abstinence has been proved to be a practice detrimental to !wait 11, and that abstal !WIN as a body are shorter lived than habitual drunkards. The doctrine thus boldly stated is fortunately preposters ous enough to defeat its ownobjers." flow preposterous, I will show.

• The statistics referred to 122 abstainers and 4,112 drinkers, or respectively 3 and 62 per cent. To give the conclusion even a fair relative vii or there ought to have been 400 abitainers. This reminds me of a story once told as a fact, concerning a detachinent of soldiers in India—that, while iiholera had struck down only 10 lair cant, of the men who drank, 50 per cent, of the teetotal- lers died. Of course, this was incredible. On referring to the return it wan found that the figures were true, but then: were only tiro abstainers to be strinik down That abstinence is conducive to longevity, we have the published opinions of mine of the leading medical men of the pas, and present. What greater authoritivi do we need than Sir William Gull, Drs. 11. W. Richardson, F. 11. ' Lees, J. J. Ridge, Norman Kerr, and a leant of others I' We could not possibly have more conclusive evidenee than that of the directors and managers of life assurance companies—keen-sighted business men, rho have given so much attention to the subject. Most of these com- panies offer extra advantages to alvteimirs, for the Jpuple reason that they live longer than liven the mode- sold t4;inkers. Many companies would not insure the no "intemperate" free drinkers" and ; 11141:114 at is considerably increased premium, on account at the entre, riot of having to pay , the sum aisured at an earlier dai4. I The Briton Company m dais is reduction of 10 per cont on the lives of allstaisiers, andthe Secretary gives aa the reason that it is done" after careful couildenyon of the experience trhieh we all hare befoee us now ' oats tin,. superiority of the lives of abstainers. 'rhe Emperor Company allows a bonus of £3 to £7 per £lOO premium, aemrding to age, to abstainers over moderate drinkers. Several other companiee make a reduction in the amount of premium, or allow a bonus to abstainers. The Blue Ribbon c;;; will not insure the hive of any but pledged teetotallers. The United Kingdom Temperance and Provident Lodi- tution ion striking instance of what I contend. It has been in existence 49 years, and comprises two sections— namely, the Temperance and the lienerul. During the 2.3 years ending 1838. the "expected" clahns in the 'rem.: perance section were were 4,235, the •• actual" claims 3,014 ; in the General section 6,516 anti 6,319 rustier- I tively ; showing that the claims in the Temperance section were leas than 71 per cent. of the " expecte:l,'. while in the General section they wean over 97 per cent.l of the "expected." ' " "' • ''

The firreptre ompany has also two sections. In the four yearn ending 1888. there were in the Temperance section 196 " expected " and 110 "actual" claims. In the General section 486, and 368 respectively. The claims of the Temperance section were thus erp4l to 58 per cent, of the " expected," in the General sMion 79 per cent. Mr. Aaron thought lit to attack yon most ungentlemanly for daring to censure his pet relieving officer, when, from the evidence placed before you nt the coroner's inquest. you could not have discharged your duty in a fair and blameless manner without so doing. When half the programins had been given there WILS an inter- val of ten minutes for refreshments. The Chairman said he was mire everyone of the audience was satisfied hy what they had men and Iteard, and it wm the inde- fatigable labour and exertion of Mrs. Wilson. and Miss Simi, that had enabled them to pass 8o enjoyable and pleasant an evening, and to those lathes the greatest praise was due. Ile hoped tine parents would .11li their children regularly and punctually to school. It not only gave satisfaction to tint managers or trustees of the. school, but conferred a great favour to themselvm and their children. They had a very good master, and an efficient staff of teacher& and he hoped the parents WOlll,l take advantage of them by carrying out his remarks. Mr. Watson, the master, said he thanked the parents fllltl friends who had so ably and willingly assisted them to give the little ones such an excellent tea. 'fliat was only the second tittle they had such an entertainment, bitt they must look forward to it being an annual one. The SKOMI ballot theprogramme toning. over, Miss Garnett distributed the mo.tifivates gained by the children in Standard I. at the last Government ,eltantination, and the meeting closed by singing the I Dosoleig„y.

YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION. Os Thursday evening, the first public meeting in contegtion with this association, was held in the Wesleyan schoolroom. The evening commenced with S tea, the trays for which had been given by several friends. The tea which was an excellent one was greatly enjoyed by a large number of people. After tea an entertainment was given, Mr. C. E. Parker officiating as chairman and, in com- mencing the meeting, ne reminded them that this association had been begun by Mrs. Coop as a means of keeping the young men from had company, and to far had suecessled. Ile confessed that a little while ago he had spokes at a meeting saying, that he thought very little about the young men of Penketh, beau's there seemed to be not one who could he said to distinguish himself. Now, however, he was forced to change his opinion for since that, the band, the art school, the gymnasium and other associations, had been formed, and seemed to be in a flourishing condition. Without further talking he would at once pro- ceed with the programme which consisted of songs by M inn Dignum, Miss James (Carlisle). Miss Garnett, Mr. It. E. Garnett and Mr. Guest. Solos and duets were also gi Vett on the cornet(Mr. Guest), violin (Miss Garnett). and fairy bells (Mr Saundullc The young men of the Gymnasium connected with the Association went through several creditable performances and added greatly to the success of the Imeeting. The exercises were with dumbells, Indian clubs and on the hortrintal bar. Mr. T. Powell con- tributed a reading. At the close Mr. It. Garnett said he rose to propose a most hearty vote of thanks to the performers that evening and also to nuns,' who had as kindly given trays at tea. He Was usually . adverse to this system of thanking people at con- certs &e., but in this case he thought they had fully deserved thanks. lie felt like Nelson who was once asked why Inc did not promote one of his men, who had been noticed for bravery and answered Oust if he were to promote all his brave men he woold have nobody hut officers. The application to the per- : formers was that all had done to well he could not menthol one above another. Mr. Watson seconded, and Mr. A. E. Garnett supported the vote of thanks, which was accorded. The Chairman then called upon Mrs. CGOI, no president to twknowledge the vote. She thanked all for their support and In- formed the Illlllll.llCl, that if any surplus was left after paving tileir debts it would go towards build- ing a room in which to hold their meetings,for they found it WAS greatly needed. The meeting then closed with the singing of the Nationel Anthem.
